claude-s · explainer-lesson

How does a hash table find one name in a million?

make a one-minute explainer on why a hash table finds a name so fast, hand-drawn in pencil like stop-motion, told by the hash table itself

What the skill did

  • Drawn in the new graphite look, measured off a hand-drawn reference: 12 fps stop-motion, three boiling drawings, whole-pixel jitter, a 1.2% exposure flicker, double-pass pencil lines, 45° hachure, a highlighter, and captions on taped paper slips.
  • Told in the first person by the hash table. Every number is real and checked against two textbooks: a list averages 500,000 looks for a million names, binary search never takes more than 20, and chaining at one name per drawer averages 1.5.
  • The drawer numbers are real FNV-1a hashes mod 16, so Ada and Tom genuinely collide in drawer 11.
  • The new kit pieces carry the story: callouts whose counts tick (1 to 500,000, then 1,000 to a billion names), routes from the hash function to each drawer, and lift(), which raises the flat row of drawers into 3D on the same coordinates.
  • A VO-led edit: every beat is placed on the word it illustrates, using Whisper word timings from the Chatterbox takes, and no beat is stretched.

Sound

  • A soft mallet bed at 84 BPM sits under the voice and rises 7 dB in the instrumental breath, while the drawers lift over a sub swell.
  • A suck-in ends exactly on the words 'hash function'. Then 0.45 s of true silence before the payoff, and a sub boom as 1.5 lands.
  • Paper and pencil foley: taps as cards land, pencil scratches as lines draw on, and ticks for every change of a counter, capped at 12 a second.
  • No stinger at the end: the bed's last note echoes on dotted eighths, 4 dB quieter and darker each time. The mix is mastered to -14 LUFS with a -1 dBTP ceiling.
